citation: Xiao & McPherson 2016 (J. Environ. Qual. 45:188)
file_in_papers: Xiao 2016 - Surface Water Storage Capacity of Twenty Tree Species in Dav.pdf
method: Rainfall simulator (3.6-139.7 mm/h, 12 intensities), 8 branch samples per species, 20 street species = 77% of Davis inventory; 40-yr interception model for 3 species
traits_or_metrics: Surface storage per unit leaf + stem surface area (mm), leaf-on / leaf-off

limits_noted: Young branch samples (likely underestimate mature trees); text and Table 4 disagree in places (abstract minimum 0.59 mm vs Bradford pear 0.51 in Table 4): Table 4 used

citation: Dowtin, Cregg, Nowak & Levia 2023 (Landsc. Urban Plan. 239:104849)
file_in_papers: Dowtin 2023 - Towards optimized runoff reduction by urban tree cover.pdf
method: Systematic review, Web of Science to 31 May 2022: 99 of 708 articles retained (7 queries, incl. one without "urban" for forest-hydrology foundations); content analysis, no meta-analysis
traits_or_metrics: Interception: LAI, canopy density/PAI, foliar hydrophobicity (inverse), leaf inclination angle (inverse), foliar roughness, bark water storage and microrelief, crown projection area, foliation period; infiltration: stemflow funnelling (erectophile branches, multi-leader crowns, smooth bark with linear furrows), permeable soils
key_quantified_results: Table 3 compiles mean interception from earlier studies: broadleaved deciduous 14.3% (Liquidambar styraciflua) to 57.9% (Ginkgo biloba), incl. Pyrus calleryana Bradford 15.0% (Xiao et al. 2000); broadleaved evergreen 16.4-68.9% (Quercus suber 27.0%); conifers 46.9-71.1%. Coniferous evergreens ~2x broadleaf evergreen and ~3x broadleaf deciduous interception capacity in Shanghai (Guo et al. 2017, as cited). Pruning: interception 46% and 65% lower in Santa Monica than in Modesto for Liquidambar and Cinnamomum (Xiao & McPherson 2002, as cited). limits_noted: Qualitative synthesis: traits are ranked by direction, not effect size; Table 3 mixes event, seasonal and annual metrics; storage thresholds mean trees become ineffective once canopy and soil saturate; traits change with age, size and health
relevance_to_topic: Trait checklist for the interception module: LAI, canopy density and crown projection area are the quantifiable ones (LiDAR); hydrophobicity, leaf angle and bark storage lack data for Porta species. Supports species selection for interception where sealing is high, and warns that pruning reduces the benefit

citation: Yang et al. 2019 (Landsc. Ecol. Eng.)
file_in_papers: The effects of tree characteristics on rainfall interception in urban.pdf
method: Throughfall under ONE street tree per species (Styphnolobium/Sophora japonica, Ginkgo biloba, Zelkova serrata, Aesculus turbinata), 6 events >= 5 mm, Sept-Oct 2018; terrestrial laser scanning for LAI, leaf area density, leaf area and angle; one-way ANOVA
traits_or_metrics: Event interception (%), whole-canopy and central-section LAI, LAD, mean leaf area, leaf angle
key_quantified_results: Mean interception: Ginkgo 57.9% (40.8-82.8), Styphnolobium 35.8% (17.2-57.1), Aesculus 30.6%, Zelkova 20.6% (9.6-30.6). LAI (p = 7.6e-5), central-section LAI (p = 0.002) and mean leaf area (p = 0.004) explain interception; leaf angle, LAD and crown shape do not; smaller leaves intercept more at similar LAI. citation: Hassan, Ghimire & Lubczynski 2017 (J. Hydrol. 555:489-505)
file_in_papers: Hassan 2017 - Remote sensing upscaling of interception loss from isolated oaks.pdf
location: Sardon catchment (80 km2), Salamanca, ES; semi-arid dehesa, mean rain 589 mm/yr

traits_or_metrics: Interception loss % of P; Gash canopy storage S, free throughfall p, canopy cover c, E/R; LAI

file_in_papers: Selbig 2022 - Quantifying the stormwater runoff volume reduction benefits of urban street tree canopy.pdf

citation: Zi, Whipple, Kauhanen & Foley 2026 (Urban Water J. 23(4):699-715; online Dec 2025)
file_in_papers: Zi 2026 - From site-scale to landscape-scale stormwater benefits of urban trees with SWMM-Canopy.pdf
method: SWMM-Canopy: i-Tree 'big-leaf' canopy interception and evaporation (wetting, saturation, drying) added to the SWMM LID module, so each tree is a GSI-like unit with canopy, surface and soil layers; sensitivity runs on a hypothetical 4,047 m2 watershed (4 tree types, 3 tree-well sizes, 1- to 25-yr 24 h storms plus RCP8.5); city-wide SWMM (54.1 km2, 215 subwatersheds, water year 2002, 282 mm); GreenPlan-IT Site Locator and Optimization Tool to compare street trees with bioretention by cost
traits_or_metrics: Max canopy storage per unit canopy area (0.76 mm broadleaf deciduous, 0.79 broadleaf evergreen, 1.24 coniferous, from Xiao & McPherson 2016; 0.26 mm leaf-off stems), LAI, extinction coefficient, ET coefficient, canopy area (mean 41.8 m2), tree-well area; runoff reduction (% of rainfall), cost per % runoff reduction
key_quantified_results: 2-yr 24 h storm (47.2 mm): impervious runoff 45.7 mm; evergreen street trees with small/medium/large wells cut runoff by 6.9/11.2/15.5%, the wells adding 1.5/3.6/5.6 mm infiltration; the canopy intercepts only 3.7% (1.8 mm) of this storm vs 14.6% of the 2002 water year. Water year 2002: over pervious ground interception is 14.6% (evergreen) vs 6.9% (deciduous) and runoff reduction 3.2% vs 1.4% of rainfall; over impervious ground, street trees (canopy + well) remove 25.1% (evergreen) and 19.5% (deciduous) of annual rainfall from runoff. Interception saturates above about the 10-yr storm. City-wide (236,335 trees, 18% canopy, all modelled as deciduous): runoff reduction 4.8% of annual rainfall (1.4-9.5% across subwatersheds). An extra 1% runoff reduction (1022 m3) costs $3.4 M less with street trees (13,811 trees) than with bioretention (274 units)
limits_noted: Transpiration not modelled; trees uniformly distributed (no clusters or overlapping crowns); roots simplified; deciduous trees modelled leaf-off (stems only); no validation of the canopy module against field data is reported (authors call the case study a proof of concept); installation cost only, no O&M; no water quality
relevance_to_topic: Closest runoff engine to ours: per-tree canopy storage plus tree-well infiltration in a Mediterranean winter-rain climate. Supports the leaf-on calendar (evergreen canopies intercept about twice as much as deciduous in the rainy season) and shows interception saturates in large storms, so the canopy term matters most for small and medium storms. Shows the gap is planning-tool integration, not physics

citation: Bartens et al. 2008 (J. Environ. Qual.)
file_in_papers: Can Urban Tree Roots Improve Infiltration through Compacted Subsoils for Stormwater Management.pdf
method: Exp 1: 30 containers, 2-yr seedlings of black oak and red maple vs no tree, clay loam compacted to 1.31 or 1.59 g/cm3, saturated, 1 L infiltration test on 6 dates (May-Sept 2006). Exp 2: green ash (n=5) vs no tree (n=5) in 78:22 stone:soil structural soil over compacted clay loam (1.63 g/cm3) behind a woven geotextile, constant-head Ksat after 2 yr
traits_or_metrics: Infiltration rate (mL/s), saturated hydraulic conductivity Ksat (cm/s), root counts
key_quantified_results: Trees raised infiltration by 63% on average (all treatments pooled) and 153% in the more compacted soil; approximate Ksat at 1.59 g/cm3: 1.3e-3 (no tree), 3.0e-3 (red maple), 3.9e-3 (black oak) cm/s, i.e. ~47, 108, 140 mm/h. Exp 2: Ksat 1.31e-3 vs 4.83e-5 cm/s with vs without green ash (27x; ~47 vs ~1.7 mm/h), P=0.008, 6.3 roots per tree through the geotextile. Black oak (coarse roots) vs red maple (fine roots): not significantly different (P 0.1-0.9 across dates). Structural soil: ~20% mineral soil, 30-35% porosity once compacted; growth-limiting dry density for clay loam 1.45-1.55 g/cm3
limits_noted: Containers, young trees (green ash 1.8 m after 2 yr), irrigated and repeatedly saturated (soil strength low, flood-tolerant species), free-draining pots, infiltration fell 53% on average across all treatments over the season (the authors suggest settling); Ksat is a relative lab value for the most restrictive layer, not a field pit rate; Platanus x acerifolia is suggested by the authors as a suitable species but was not tested
relevance_to_topic: Roots do raise infiltration through compacted subsoil, but the root-architecture (species) effect is NOT shown: keeps roots out of the species scoring. Gives a lab range for a pit-infiltration sensitivity and the structural-soil specification (stone:soil 78:22, 30-35% porosity) for the soil option on backup slide B1

file_in_papers: Nyelele 2021 - A multi-objective decision support framework to prioritize tree planting locations.pdf
method: Linear programming (lpSolve in R) over 1,132 census block groups (2,264 decision variables: m2 of new canopy on plantable pervious and plantable impervious land per block group); 14 scenarios that maximise one or more benefits (PM2.5 removal $, avoided runoff $, heat index reduction K, canopy, poverty- or race-weighted canopy) under a $400 M budget, a 26% canopy goal, a Gini equality target and/or a 10% minimum canopy; benefit coefficients per m2 of canopy from i-Tree Eco, Hydro and Cool (2010 conditions); constraint method for a Pareto front (Gini 0.22-0.31)

method: Thermal camera (FLIR T640, 1 m height) over asphalt, porphyry cobbles and grass in the shade of 332 solitary trees of 85 species; 1,005 cooling records at the west edge, centre and east edge of each shadow; 8 clear days, 11:00-16:00; cooling = sunlit reference minus shaded surface temperature; day and time-of-day adjusted values only for categorical comparisons and COOLrate; multiple linear regression on unadjusted cooling (80/20 train/test, AIC stepwise) and relative importance (lmg)
traits_or_metrics: Surface cooling dT (and time-adjusted dTadj); LAIcept (ceptometer estimate of light penetration), crown diameter, tree and crown height, vertical and horizontal gap fraction, leaf colour lightness, leaf shape, size and arrangement, crown shape; COOLrate = dTadj at the west edge / crown diameter
key_quantified_results: Median average cooling at west / centre / east edge of the shadow (Table 2): asphalt 16.4 / 15.1 / 10.5 C, porphyry 12.9 / 11.8 / 6.7 C, grass 8.5 / 9.1 / 7.8 C. Median maximum surface temperature sun vs west shade: asphalt 46.3 vs 28.3 C, porphyry 49.4 vs 29.7, grass 43.2 vs 25.3 (about 18-20 C lower). Largest single value 26.8 C (asphalt, west edge, 14:00, 8 m Carpinus betulus, LAIcept 3.92, crown width 6 m). The text calls LAIcept by far the most important variable, but in Table 3 it has the largest relative importance in only 2 of 9 models (asphalt centre 25.4%, grass west 22.4%) and is in the top five in 7 of 9; GAP2, air temperature, log volume, leaf lightness and grass cover lead the others, and LAIcept is absent from the asphalt-west and porphyry-centre regression models. No single crown-dimension measure stood out; crown width classes differed significantly for asphalt (ANOVA p = 0.03; porphyry not, grass not reported); tree height mattered less than crown width. Needle-leaved conifers gave high dT but narrow shadows (lower COOLrate); sympodial tiered and weeping crowns gave the lowest COOLrate. Authors recommend high LAI with wide, continuous crowns (e.g. Morus alba small, Fagus sylvatica large)

relevance_to_topic: Italian 85-species dataset (per-tree traits are in the supplementary data, not yet obtained): possible source of species shade parameters. Leaf-on only, so it says nothing about the winter shade cost. Differs from Kaluarachchi 2020 (#45), who found no LAI effect on dTs in Sydney with a different LAI method (canopy imager per tree vs ceptometer per shadow position)

file_in_papers: Morabito 2021 - Surface urban heat islands in Italian metropolitan cities.pdf
location: 10 Italian metropolitan cities incl. Florence and Bologna
method: MODIS MOD11A2 summer daytime LST 2016-2018 (1 km, resampled to 250 m); ISPRA 10 m impervious layer (2017) and a Sentinel-1/2 10 m tree-cover layer (2017); 300 m focal densities reclassified into low/medium/high impervious x tree-cover classes (USLAND, 9 classes); SUHI slopes = LST change per 10% more of a class in the metropolitan core (or less outside it), by elevation stratum
traits_or_metrics: Summer daytime LST; SUHI; impervious and tree-cover density classes
key_quantified_results: High-impervious/low-tree areas (HI_LT) are warmest and low-impervious/high-tree areas (LI_HT) coolest. Inland cities: LST difference between high and low impervious density 4.5-7.1 C, between low and high tree cover 1.4-4.7 C. Plain areas: +10% HI_LT in the core raises SUHI by 3.2 C in Bologna (largest among inland cities) and 0.8 C in Naples; Florence ranks next after Bologna (2.9 C); Turin hill areas 4.0 C. +10% low-impervious tree-covered area lowers LST by 0.5 C (Milan, Turin) to 0.2 C (Bari, Rome). Bologna and Florence cores have compact HI_LT patterns (about 10-20% of the core)
limits_noted: Surface (not air) temperature, daytime summer only; 1 km MODIS resampled to 250 m; only impervious surfaces and tree cover considered; 300 m focal radius chosen by the authors
relevance_to_topic: Florence and Bologna are inland cities where low tree cover in the core drives the largest SUHI slopes: supports tree cover as the lever, at city scale only (no species or positions)

citation: Mannucci et al. 2025 (City Environ. Interact.)
file_in_papers: Mannucci 2025 - A parametric integrated workflow to assess multi-domain heat.pdf

traits_or_metrics: UTCI, surface runoff
key_quantified_results: LBT vs ENVI-met UTCI MBE 0.8-2.3 C, CVRMSE 7-13%; MRT MBE 2.4-5.9 C, CVRMSE 22-38% (worst under direct sun, up to +8.65 C UTCI at 7-8 h); peak UTCI 29-41 C; LBT treats trees as shade only and likely underestimates vegetation cooling by ~2-3 C; CN runoff depth ~95.5 mm for the design event
limits_noted: Scenario testing only; no species traits, no optimisation; particle runoff not calibrated; no CFD wind
relevance_to_topic: CLOSEST PRECEDENT for heat + runoff in Grasshopper (confirmed in full text). Also the Ladybug-vs-ENVI-met validation reference for our heat module

citation: Shaamala et al. 2025 (Cities)
file_in_papers: Shaamala 2025 - Algorithmic urban greening for thermal resilience AI-optimis.pdf

citation: Eslami, Van Cauwenbergh, Rezazadeh Helmi & van Griensven 2025 (13th Urban Drainage Modelling Conference, Innsbruck, Sept 2025; extended abstract, 3 pp.; the search record dates it 2026)

citation: Liang, Zhang, Zeng & Shen 2021 (Sci. Total Environ. 779:146415)
file_in_papers: Liang 2021 - Land-use decision approach integrating thermal regulation and stormwater management.pdf
location: Xiamen, CN (1699 km2; subtropical marine monsoon, 1530 mm/yr)
method: City-scale land-use optimisation: 1 km sampling units (size chosen by Shannon diversity of land use); Landsat LST (one summer 2017 scene) and SCS-CN runoff for a 50-yr storm (222.91 mm) regressed on the area of 6 land-cover classes (adj. R2 0.787 and 0.821); NSGA-II minimising LST and runoff and maximising land economic output; units classed into 4 urbanisation stages (construction density x ANN construction probability); Pareto solutions clustered by k-means into land-use area ranges per stage

citation: Dong, Ye, Su, Haase & Lausch 2026 (npj Urban Sustain. 6:47)
file_in_papers: Dong 2026 - Optimizing urban tree species composition to maximize nature-based solutions.pdf; Dong supplementary tables.pdf
read_level: full text (11 Oct, open PDF; supplement read 13 Oct)
method: Species-composition optimisation: demand maps (stormwater from flood susceptibility; heat from LST; also air quality, carbon) x species effectiveness from i-Tree Eco (30 most common local species), NSGA-III (pop 400, 500 gen, 4 objectives) + TOPSIS; decision variable = species proportions per location, bounded by available canopy space

Platanus x acerifolia (12.88% of Philadelphia's trees) and Pyrus calleryana (5.72%) are Pareto-dominated, i.e. 'functionally inferior' on all four services in i-Tree terms; the five most recommended species (Acer saccharinum, A. rubrum, Liquidambar styraciflua, A. saccharum, Liriodendron tulipifera) make up 85% of the optimal mix. citation: Langenheim & White 2022 (Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 19:8220)
file_in_papers: Langenheim 2022 - Green infrastructure and urban-renewal simulation for street tree design.pdf
location: Arden-Macaulay urban renewal, Melbourne, AU (20 m streets, 6-storey street walls, H:W 1:1, bearing N 7 E)

citation: Schrodi, Briegel, Argus, Christen & Brox 2023 (arXiv:2310.05691, preprint)
file_in_papers: Schrodi 2023 - Climate-sensitive urban planning through optimization of tree placements.pdf
location: Freiburg im Breisgau, DE (five 500 x 500 m areas at 1 m: city centre, new/medium-age/old residential, industrial)
method: U-Net surrogates trained on SOLWEIG predict point-wise Tmrt (L1 error 1.93 K) and directly the time-aggregated Tmrt for a day, week, year or decade; a second U-Net updates vegetation sky view factor from the vegetation DSM; tree positions optimised by iterated local search (greedy top-K start, GA perturbation, hill climbing); uniform trees (12 m, 9 m crown); also relocation of existing trees for the hottest week of 2020
traits_or_metrics: Mean radiant temperature (aggregated), hours with Tmrt > 60 C; tree positions; fixed tree geometry and transmissivity
key_quantified_results: Up to 400,000x faster than per-hour evaluation (decade case). 50 added trees (4050 m2, 1.62% of area): area-mean Tmrt change -0.30 K/m2 (day), -0.23 (week), -0.03 (year and decade), better than random, greedy and GA baselines. Trees lower Tmrt by day and in summer but raise it at night and in winter; a rule 'trees cool when incoming shortwave > 96 W/m2' classifies the sign with 97.9% accuracy. Diminishing returns with more or taller trees. Added trees go mainly to east-west streets and large paved spaces; relocating existing trees would cut mean Tmrt by 0.83 K and hours above 60 C by 19.7% in the heatwave week, moving trees from already shaded spots to sealed plazas and parking lots
limits_noted: Authors: one city, static city, uniform tree geometry, species and transmissivity (SOLWEIG limit), no feasibility, ownership or pedestrian-use constraints; Tmrt only (no air temperature, wind, humidity). Preprint
relevance_to_topic: Strong precedent for the heat side of the layout optimiser: placement matters as much as tree count, summer benefit vs winter cost is real (supports the seasonal shade weighting in the heat proxy), and E-W streets and sealed plazas are priority sites. No species choice, no runoff, so the dual-objective gap remains

citation: Orta-Ortiz & Geneletti 2022 (Environ. Impact Assess. Rev. 95:106802)
file_in_papers: Orta-Ortiz 2022 - What variables matter when designing nature-based solutions for stormwater management.pdf
method: Literature review (Web of Science, 2009-2021): 707 hits, 104 read in full, 57 with evidence on design variables of urban forests, parks, street trees and community gardens for runoff mitigation and stormwater treatment
traits_or_metrics: 13 design variables (authors' count; Table 2 lists 14 rows): vegetation (species, canopy cover, tree density, understory complexity, vegetation arrangement), soil (type, porosity, organic matter, raised beds), physical (tree-pit area and elevation, runoff trench, underdrain), location in the watershed

citation: Li, Feng, Sun, Li, Yu & Fang 2023 (Build. Environ. 228:109846)
file_in_papers: Li 2023 - STMRT A simple tree canopy radiative transfer model for outdoor mean radiant temperature.pdf
location: Model (validated on one isolated Freeman maple, Utah, US; scenarios for Shanghai, CN)
method: Simple tree-canopy radiative transfer model (STMRT) for mean radiant temperature under a canopy: direct and diffuse shortwave transmissivity by a Beer-Lambert law with the leaf-angle projection G and leaf transmissivity, canopy longwave from air temperature; validated against measured PAR under one tree (Bailey 2013 data) and compared with 4SAIL; leaf-angle data for 126 species

location: Florence and Naples, IT (one summer scene each, 10 and 21 Jul 2016)
method: One Landsat 8 OLI/TIRS scene per city; LST from band 10 with NDVI-based emissivity; NDVI, NDBI and land-cover classification (ISODATA + maximum likelihood, kappa 0.89); UHI = LST > mean + 0.5 SD; hot spots LST > mean + 2 SD; urban thermal field variance index; LST checked against MODIS (r 0.61 for Florence)
traits_or_metrics: LST, NDVI, NDBI, UHI and non-UHI zones, UTFVI
key_quantified_results: Florence mean LST 32.84 C, UHI threshold 33.81 C; UHI zones 3.15 C warmer than non-UHI (Naples 3.31 C) and cover 35.93% of Florence; 76.62% of the UHI area lies on built-up or bare land. Citywide LST vs NDVI r = -0.71 and vs NDBI r = 0.71 (Florence), weaker inside UHI zones (-0.38 and 0.21). Built-up and bare land 39.91% of Florence
limits_noted: One clear-sky scene per city; surface, not air, temperature; UHI defined statistically within the city, no rural reference; no in-situ validation
relevance_to_topic: Florence heat-island context (cited in city_screening.md); no tree or species detail

citation: Niccoli, Borghi & Chirici 2026 (Boll. Soc. Geogr. Ital. ser. 14, 9(1):85-104)
file_in_papers: Niccoli 2026 - Mapping Local Climate Zones and temperature dynamics in the Metropolitan Area of Florence.pdf
method: 20 m Local Climate Zone map by Random Forest on 5 Sentinel-2 dates plus building height, sky view factor, building fraction, imperviousness and canopy height (WUDAPT training; overall accuracy 93.85%); seasonal Landsat 8 LST 2022-2023 by LCZ; 251 Netatmo citizen stations (2.3 M hourly values Jan 2023-Jul 2024 after CrowdQC+), dominant LCZ in a 150 m-diameter buffer; tropical (> 20 C) and very warm (> 24 C) nights
traits_or_metrics: LST and air temperature by LCZ; share of tropical and very warm nights
key_quantified_results: Summer median LST: dense trees 36.8 C and water 37.0 C vs compact mid-rise 46.3 C, compact low-rise 46.0 C and large low-rise 45.8 C; scattered trees 42.2 C. Summer nights: compact mid-rise median air temperature 24.2 C vs open low-rise 22.8 C and scattered trees 22.2 C; tropical nights 62.4% (compact mid-rise) vs 44.5% (open low-rise) and 46.5% (scattered trees); nights > 24 C 24.1% vs 7.2% (scattered trees). By day scattered trees (27.7 C) are about as warm as the urban LCZs (27.6-28.4 C); the authors find no marked cooling. Florence: 45% urban LCZs, dense trees 8.9% of the municipality
limits_noted: No citizen stations in dense-tree or water LCZs; citizen-sensor biases despite quality control; citizen data Jan 2023-Jul 2024 (tropical nights: summer 2023 and 1 Jun-20 Jul 2024); seasonal mean LST; LCZs are neighbourhood-scale, not street-scale
relevance_to_topic: Florence night-time evidence: the scattered-trees LCZ (in the Piana largely olive groves) has fewer tropical nights than compact mid-rise (46.5% vs 62.4%), an LCZ-scale association that our daytime heat proxy does not capture; Florence's 3-30-300 Piano del Verde as policy context

citation: Coutts, White, Tapper, Beringer & Livesley 2016 (Theor. Appl. Climatol. 124:55-68; online Feb 2015)
file_in_papers: Coutts 2016 - Temperature and human thermal comfort effects of street trees across three contrasting street canyons.pdf
method: Three east-west streets: a deep CBD canyon (H:W 0.76, 31% canopy, Platanus), a shallow open street (H:W 0.27, 12%) and a shallow treed street (H:W 0.32, 45%, Ulmus parvifolia); 10, 5 and 7 pole stations at 3.5-4 m (air temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation, globe temperature), May 2011-Jun 2013; UTCI from RayMan; heat events Jan-Feb 2012 and Mar 2013
traits_or_metrics: Canyon air temperature, mean radiant temperature, UTCI, sky view factor (buildings vs trees)
key_quantified_results: In heat events the treed street was 0.2-0.6 C cooler than the open street by day, 0.9 C at 9-10 am and up to 1.5 C (differences not significant). Trees cut UTCI mainly through mean radiant temperature, from 'very strong' (> 38 C) to 'strong'; on a 41.1 C day unshaded stations exceeded 46 C UTCI while shaded ones stayed 'very strong'. Canopies slightly raise night-time UTCI (still comfortable). The deep canyon was up to 4.8 C warmer than the treed street before dawn and buildings masked tree effects there. Daytime UTCI rises with sky view factor; streets with SVF > 0.5 should get trees first, on the sun-exposed side of east-west streets
limits_noted: Three streets in one city; sensors at 3.5-4 m, not pedestrian height; most air temperature differences not significant; two genera (Platanus x acerifolia and P. occidentalis in the CBD, Ulmus parvifolia in the treed street)
relevance_to_topic: Direct placement rules for the heat proxy: weight positions by sun exposure / sky view factor (SVF > 0.5), favour the sun-exposed side of east-west streets, expect little gain in deep canyons; the night-time penalty is small

citation: Smithers, Doick, Burton, Sibille, Steinbach, Harris, Groves & Blicharska 2018 (Urban Ecosyst. 21:851-862)
file_in_papers: Smithers 2018 - Comparing the relative abilities of tree species to cool the urban environment.pdf
method: Literature review plus semi-structured interviews with 7 experts; simplified surface energy balance (QH + dQS = Q* - QE) and scenario diagrams; relative indices to compare species
traits_or_metrics: Crown diameter, LAI, canopy aspect ratio (crown height / crown diameter), tree height, stomatal conductance or growth rate, albedo
key_quantified_results: Relative indices: transpiration ~ crown diameter x LAI x canopy aspect ratio x (stomatal conductance or growth rate); reflection ~ albedo x crown diameter x LAI; shading ~ crown diameter x LAI x tree height / canopy aspect ratio. Default albedo 0.1 for conifers and 0.2 for broadleaves (ranges 0.05-0.20 vs 0.09-0.36). Experts judged rainfall interception unlikely to affect the UHI in temperate regions. Advice: favour large, fast-growing or drought-tolerant species with high albedo; age, health and pruning reduce cooling
limits_noted: No empirical test and no weighting between mechanisms; relative scores only; temperate focus; assumes species compared at the same site
relevance_to_topic: Precedent for trait-based species scoring of cooling with the same traits as our heat proxy (crown diameter, LAI, height, aspect ratio); unvalidated, so our proxy still needs the Ladybug UTCI check

citation: Rahman, Moser, Rotzer & Pauleit 2019 (Urban Ecosyst. 22:683-697)
file_in_papers: Rahman 2019 - Comparing the transpirational and shading effects of two contrasting urban tree species.pdf
method: 10 Tilia cordata and 10 Robinia pseudoacacia street trees in grass lawns beside asphalt (Messestadt Riem); sap flow (Granier), LAI from hemispherical photos, air temperature at 1.5 m and 4.5 m under canopies vs open, soil moisture; sun-shade surface temperature over grass and asphalt on 8 clear days (9:00-18:00)
traits_or_metrics: LAI, sap flux density, transpiration energy loss, within-canopy and near-ground air cooling, sun-shade surface temperature difference
key_quantified_results: T. cordata: higher LAI (3.64 vs 2.61, Table 1; '30% higher' in the abstract), sap flux density 0.09 vs 0.05 ml/cm2/min, about 3x transpiration, energy loss 1.9 vs 0.6 kW per tree (9:00-18:00); daytime within-canopy cooling 1.6 vs 0.9 C. Surface cooling over asphalt 25.59 vs 12.71 C, over grass 9 vs 8 C (not different). Per unit LAI about 6 C of surface cooling over asphalt vs 3 C over grass (r 0.72 vs 0.30). Near-ground air over grass was cooler under the sparser, water-efficient R. pseudoacacia
limits_noted: Two species, two plots, one summer; surface temperature by hand-held laser; asphalt shade measured under 5 other Robinia trees
relevance_to_topic: Supports LAI-weighted shade and surface-dependent weighting (asphalt about twice grass); suggests sparse, water-efficient species can suit lawns. Pairs with Rahman 2020 (#44)

citation: Paravantis, Santamouris, Cartalis, Efthymiou & Kontoulis 2017 (Sustainability 9:606)
file_in_papers: Paravantis 2017 - Mortality associated with high ambient temperatures, heatwaves and the urban heat island in Athens.pdf
method: Daily cardiovascular and respiratory deaths of people over 65 in the municipality of Athens (Hellenic Statistical Authority) vs temperature and humidity at one central station (Patission St.); exposure-response comparisons, OLS, Poisson and negative binomial time series; cluster and discriminant analysis of May-September days
traits_or_metrics: Daily deaths over 65; Tmax, Tmin, apparent temperature, humidity, heatwave days
key_quantified_results: U-shaped exposure-response. Mean daily deaths 11.69 vs 10.69 on the 303 days with Tmax >= 35 C (+9%) and 14.42 vs 10.75 on the 12 days >= 40 C (+34%, p = 0.016) (Table 2); the abstract summarises this as +20-35%. Cold days also raise deaths (Tmin <= 0 C: 12.85 vs 10.75, +19.5%). One-day lag of Tmax; the time-series models fit poorly. Excess mortality +23% in the hottest-day cluster and +20.6% in the heatwave cluster
limits_noted: City-wide counts and one station, so the urban heat island is not separated spatially; poor model fit; only cardiovascular and respiratory deaths over 65
relevance_to_topic: Health stakes of heat in a Mediterranean city (cited in city_screening.md); also shows cold-day mortality, a reminder that winter shade has a cost

citation: Sharmin, Tjoelker, Pfautsch, Esperon-Rodriguez, Rymer & Power 2023 (Urban For. Urban Green. 83:127913)
file_in_papers: Sharmin 2023 - Tree crown traits and planting context contribute to reducing urban heat.pdf
location: Greater Sydney, AU (5 suburbs, humid subtropical; Jan-Mar 2019)
method: 470 trees of 61 species (of 490/63 measured) in three planting contexts (park, nature strip, asphalt); air temperature at 1.5 m (Kestrel) and surface temperature (IR thermometer) of standard black/white tiles and artificial grass plus natural grass, shade vs adjacent full sun, 10:00-16:00 on days >25 C; tree LAI (LAI-2200), height, DBH, crown depth and width, clear stem height; linear mixed models with species and suburb as random effects
traits_or_metrics: LAI, crown width, crown depth, tree height, DBH, clear stem height; sun-shade air and surface temperature difference (dT); planting context
key_quantified_results: Air dT mean 1.1 C, max 3.7 C. Surface dT mean 28.1 C black tiles (max 46.1), 27.9 C artificial grass (max 51.9), 11.4 C white tiles (max 25.9), 12.9 C natural grass; the abstract says 'up to 45 C', the results give these maxima. Shaded tile temperatures were lower in parks and nature strips than in asphalt settings (e.g. black 32.1 vs 34.6 C), but dT did not differ among contexts. LAI explained little: air dT R2 0.11 (about 1.1 C per unit LAI, 'weak coefficient'), black tiles R2 0.20, artificial grass R2 0.25; LAI-dT links significant in asphalt and park, not in nature strips. No trait related to natural-grass dT; canopy width related to air dT only in parks (R2 0.35)
limits_noted: Species and tree sizes not balanced across contexts; shade and transpiration effects not separated; some park data on days >35 C; hand-held point measurements; Sydney summer only
relevance_to_topic: Supports LAI and crown width as shade-proxy inputs but shows they explain only 10-25% of the variance; surface type (dark vs light vs grass) matters as much as species. Backs weighting shade by ground surface (see Rahman 2019 #102, Kaluarachchi #45). Heat only

citation: Alves, Formiga & Traldi 2018 (Urban Ecosyst. 21:697-706)
file_in_papers: Alves 2018 - Rainfall interception capacity of tree species used in urban afforestation.pdf
location: Uruacu, Goias, BR (tropical Aw; Oct 2012-Mar 2013, gauges stated elsewhere as Nov 2012-Apr 2013)
method: 9 trees of 4 species (Mangifera indica, Pachira aquatica, Licania tomentosa, Caesalpinia peltophoroides) on a 7200 m2 site; 1-min tipping-bucket pluviographs under canopies (moved every 15 days) vs one open-field gauge; interception = gross minus under-canopy rainfall; 55 of 182 events with >5 mm; canopy dimensions measured, LAI from an earlier destructive survey
traits_or_metrics: Event interception (mm, %), canopy volume, leaf area, LAI, canopy projection area; rainfall depth, duration, intensity
key_quantified_results: Mean event 16.7 mm; mean interception M. indica 8.0 mm, P. aquatica 7.4, L. tomentosa 7.2, C. peltophoroides 4.8 (all trees 6.9 mm). Mean LAI mango 1.5, munguba 1.3, oiti 0.6, sibipiruna 0.1 (text; Table 1 garbled in extraction). Small events (<10 mm, <60 min, <10 mm/h): 2.7-4.5 mm intercepted; large events (mean 32.3 mm, 17.4 mm/h): 5.9-10 mm. Interception is about 40% of rain in short, light events and, as stated, 'about 3.6%' in intense long ones. Cites i-Tree Streets and the Green Values Calculator using a fixed 1.0 mm canopy storage for all species (via Berland & Hopton 2014)
limits_noted: 9 trees, single site, partly overlapping canopies; gauge-under-canopy method (stemflow ignored); LAI taken from another study; asymptotic fit Eq. 1 given without fitted parameters
relevance_to_topic: Species-level interception differences track leaf area and LAI, supporting an LAI-scaled storage term; the fixed 1 mm storage of i-Tree tools is the baseline the trait approach improves on. Tropical species, so values do not transfer to Barcelona

citation: Gotsch, Draguljic & Williams 2018 (Urban Ecosyst. 21:183-195; online 2017)
file_in_papers: Gotsch 2018 - Effectiveness of urban trees to mitigate storm water runoff via transpiration and stemflow.pdf
location: Lancaster, Pennsylvania, US (3 parks; May-Sep 2015, a wet summer)
method: Heat-ratio sap flow on 7 large park trees of 4 species (DBH 51-91 cm) and 7 small trees of 7 species (DBH 5-10 cm); 15 post-nocturnal-rain dry periods; max flow, daily flow, max slope S and lag D vs solar radiation; mixed models of microclimate drivers; stemflow, throughfall (3 gauges per tree), branch angle and crown leaf area on the small trees
traits_or_metrics: Sap flow rate and daily volume, response slope and lag after rain, branch angle, crown leaf area, stemflow and throughfall:stemflow ratio
key_quantified_results: Large trees: max sap flow from <5 to >20 L/h; Platanus occidentalis highest S (order of magnitude above Fraxinus americana, 4-5x higher max and daily flow); lag median 0-1 h except one maple at 3 h (Results name Acer saccharum, the Discussion names Acer rubrum). Small trees: Acer griseum and Zelkova serrata 5-7x the flow of Parrotia and Ginkgo; no lag differences. Drivers: solar radiation for large trees, relative humidity for small (model r2 0.84/0.86). Steeper branch angles gave more stemflow relative to throughfall; crown leaf area was not related to that ratio
limits_noted: Few trees per species (1-2 large), park trees not street trees, wet summer so no drought signal; stemflow only on small trees; no runoff volume computed
relevance_to_topic: Species differ several-fold in post-storm transpiration and in stemflow routing (branch angle), but the paper gives no runoff numbers; supports transpiration and branch angle as secondary traits, not usable as model parameters. Humid-temperate, not Mediterranean

citation: Farrell, Livesley, Arndt et al. 2022 (Urban For. Urban Green. 76:127732)
file_in_papers: Farrell 2022 - Can we integrate ecological approaches to improve plant selection for green infrastructure.pdf
location: Review; case study in 10 Australian cities ('Which Plant Where' Living Lab)
method: Narrative review and plant-selection framework: infer tolerance (heat, drought, pests, invasiveness) and function (stormwater, cooling, air quality, biodiversity) from plant traits and from species' natural distribution (habitat templates, climate envelopes); case study list built from inventories of 22 Australian urban areas
traits_or_metrics: Drought traits (wood density, turgor loss point, SLA, succulence), heat traits (leaf size and thickness), transpiration traits (Huber value, growth rate), canopy width, density and leaf orientation for shade; leaf area for interception; climate niche
key_quantified_results: No new measurements. Case study: 1342 tree and 34 shrub species compiled, filtered to 62 common to at least 10 urban areas, 30 more excluded by the working group, final 8 trees and 8 shrubs chosen by nursery availability and contrasting climate of origin. Cited ranges: lethal leaf temperature 41.5-50.8 C; urban leaves can exceed 65 C. Platanus x acerifolia and Pyrus calleryana flagged as losing leaves after extreme heat
limits_noted: Not exhaustive; no spatial scale or prioritisation; traits were not yet used to select the case-study species; Living Lab results pending
relevance_to_topic: Framework precedent for trait-based species filtering (tolerance first, then function), close to the palette-plus-constraints step of the tool. Gives no trait-to-service numbers; heat and drought tolerance criteria fit Barcelona

citation: Farrell, Szota, Williams & Arndt 2013 (Plant Soil 372:177-193)
file_in_papers: Farrell 2013 - High water users can be drought tolerant.pdf
method: Pot experiment (4 L, scoria green-roof substrate), 12 granite-outcrop species (4 monocots, 4 herbs, 4 shrubs) plus the succulent Sedum pachyphyllum; well-watered vs water deficit (20% of well-watered use) for 50 days; gravimetric transpiration, pre-dawn and midday leaf water potential, relative water content, root mass fraction, LAR, SLA
traits_or_metrics: Daily transpiration per pot and per leaf area, transpiration under deficit as % of well-watered, pre-dawn water potential, root mass fraction, leaf area ratio, SLA, succulence
key_quantified_results: Well-watered transpiration ranged from 4.3 g/pot/day (Sedum) to 125.7 (Isotoma axillaris), mean 52.1; outcrop species transpired 9.6-58.8x more than Sedum per unit leaf area. The 4 monocots and I. axillaris kept pre-dawn water potential above -1.5 MPa under deficit by cutting transpiration to 23-28% of their control; the shrubs and three herbs fell to -2.2 to -5.2 MPa. High absolute root mass fraction went with better water status (R2 0.36); changes in RMF, LAR and SLA did not. Plant size (leaf area), not per-leaf rate, drove pot water use
limits_noted: Glasshouse pots, young plants, one substrate; deficit scaled to each species' own use; no runoff measured; green-roof herbs and shrubs, not trees
relevance_to_topic: Low direct relevance (green roofs, no trees). Supports the general rule 'high water use when wet, stomatal control when dry' as a selection trait pair for stormwater plants; cited by Farrell 2022 (#107) and Thom 2022 (#79)

citation: Yan, Wang, Liao, Xu & Wan 2021 (J. Hydrol. 592:125807)
file_in_papers: Yan 2021 - Effects of the morphological characteristics of plants on rainfall interception.pdf
location: Guizhou karst, CN (subtropical evergreen broadleaf forest; not urban)
method: (1) Water adsorbed on 1-cm standard branches with leaves of 116 woody species after a 150 mm spray (upper surface only, and upper+lower by rotating the branch); (2) rainfall simulator (25 m2, 4 m drop) over one small tree (<3.5 m) of each of 4 species, 5 events of 10 min at 8.8-69.8 mm/h; throughfall containers, spiral stemflow collars, interception by difference; LAI, mean tilt angle, DIFN (LAI-2000), mean leaf area, leaf shape factor; raindrop sizes by filter-paper stain
traits_or_metrics: Adsorbed water (% of branch+leaf mass), leaf habit, leaf texture, trichomes, mean leaf area, leaf shape factor, LAI, mean foliage tilt angle, DIFN; interception, throughfall and stemflow rates; drop size D50, kinetic energy
key_quantified_results: 116 species: mean adsorbed water 15.4% (upper surface) and 24.8% (both surfaces) of branch+leaf mass. Trichomes 36.6% vs 20.1% without; papery 28.8% vs leathery 21.7%; deciduous 28.2% vs evergreen 22.5%. Total leaf area explained about 45% of adsorbed water. Simulator (4 species): interception 12.7-19.6% of rain, throughfall 65.7-83.2%, stemflow 2.4-16.5%; interception vs LAI R2 0.84 (also mean leaf area R2 0.41, shape factor R2 0.42); throughfall and stemflow tied to canopy gap fraction DIFN (R2 0.93, 0.83). Under-canopy drop kinetic energy about 12.5-20 J/m2/mm vs 7.98 in the open
limits_noted: Adsorption test gives a maximum storage proxy, not real interception; simulator on one small tree per species with LAI only 0.5-0.8 and evaporation ignored; non-urban karst forest species
relevance_to_topic: Trait evidence for interception beyond LAI: trichomes, papery leaves and leaf area raise water storage; per-tree interception scaled with LAI (R2 0.84, 4 trees). Supports an LAI-scaled storage term with optional leaf-surface modifiers; species are subtropical Chinese, values not transferable

citation: Nytch, Melendez-Ackerman, Perez & Ortiz-Zayas 2019 (Urban Ecosyst. 22:103-115; online 2018)
file_in_papers: Nytch 2019 - Rainfall interception by six urban trees in San Juan, Puerto Rico.pdf
location: San Juan, Puerto Rico (humid subtropical; Aug-Dec 2014)
method: 6 open or semi-open trees (3 evergreen Calophyllum antillanum, 3 deciduous Albizia procera) in a botanical garden; throughfall by gutters into tipping buckets 1 m from the bole vs a rooftop control; 13 storms (2.9-72.4 mm, 1-129 h); stemflow ignored; leaf area from DBH allometry of proxy species; repeated-measures models with storm intensity class
traits_or_metrics: Relative interception loss, throughfall %, throughfall delay; leaf area (allometric), crown size; max hourly intensity, wind
key_quantified_results: Mean interception 19.6% across all trees (abstract: 19.7%); Albizia 22.8% vs Calophyllum 16.4% in the Results (abstract: 22.7% and 16.7%). Range -21.7% to 79.1% per tree and storm; two largest storms only 10.3% and 6.4%, two of the smallest (storms 12 and 13) 60.9% and 40.0%. Tree type mattered for low and moderate storms but not for heavy ones (>7.6 mm/h); negative interception only at >=11 mm/h (wind, drip points). Albizia had about double the estimated leaf area (78.5 vs 41.5 m2). Cites Xiao & McPherson 2002: summer 47% vs winter 16% interception in Santa Monica
limits_noted: Six trees, two species, one season; one gauge-and-gutter set per tree; stemflow omitted; leaf area from proxy allometries; wind-driven rain biases
relevance_to_topic: Supports storm-dependent saturation: species differences shrink in intense storms, so trait-based interception gains are largest for frequent small storms, not the design storm. Use when framing which return periods the runoff module can claim

citation: Zabret & Sraj 2019 (Water 11:2659)
file_in_papers: Zabret 2019 - Influence of rain event characteristics on rainfall interception by urban trees.pdf
read_level: full text (12 Oct; text layer partly garbled, numbers read from the clean passages)
method: Throughfall (trough and roving funnel gauges) and stemflow under two Betula pendula and two Pinus nigra; open-area gauge and rooftop optical disdrometer (drop size and number); 176 of 413 events with complete data; multiple correspondence analysis of rainfall amount, duration, intensity, wind speed and direction, median volume diameter (MVD) and raindrop number
traits_or_metrics: Interception ratio I/P per event; LAI (birch 2.6 leafed, pine 3.9), canopy cover, bark storage (birch 0.7 mm, pine 3.5 mm); rainfall and drop-size descriptors, wind
key_quantified_results: 176 events, 2050 mm, mean 2.8 mm/h, 8.3 h. Total interception 23.7% (birch) and 46.9% (pine); event medians 36% and 75%. Throughfall 73% (birch) and 53% (pine) of gross rain; stemflow 3.3% (birch), about 0.06% (pine). I/P below 10% in 16 birch events and 2 pine events. MCA: I/P falls with events >6 mm and >1.8 mm/h; larger drops (MVD >1.5 mm) and more drops cut interception, pine gains with small drops; nearby buildings create wind corridors that lower interception for both species
limits_noted: Two trees per species in one park; disdrometer on a roof 50 m away; MCA is descriptive (categorical thresholds), not predictive
relevance_to_topic: Confirms the conifer-vs-broadleaf deciduous gap (about 47% vs 24%) and that interception share collapses in large, intense events; supports a saturating storage model rather than a fixed percentage. Pairs with Zabret 2018 (#116) and Zabret & Sraj 2019 (#7)

citation: Xu, Zhu, Tan et al. 2025 (Sustainability 17:7793)
file_in_papers: Xu 2025 - Urban-scale quantification of rainfall interception drivers in tree communities.pdf
location: Zhengzhou, CN (123 parks, 805 plots of 0.04 ha; temperate semi-arid monsoon, 542 mm/yr)
method: i-Tree Eco plot survey (July 2021; 17,626 trees, 99 species) to model annual rainfall interception per tree (ARI) and per plot green area (RIE); 3 leaf types and 7 community types; ANOVA, Pearson correlation and stepwise regression on 20 morphological, ecological and diversity factors
traits_or_metrics: Annual interception per tree (m3/yr) and per area (mm/yr); mean tree height, crown width, DBH, branch height, relative height, cover, planting density, importance value, diversity indices
key_quantified_results: Park mean RIE 66.35 mm/yr (plots 0.25-547.5); mean ARI 1.23 m3/tree/yr, about 553,000 m3/yr city-wide (modelled). Deciduous broadleaf trees highest ARI (1.28 m3/yr; Paulownia fortunei 5.50, Populus tomentosa 4.41, Zelkova serrata 3.83; one Platanus orientalis 32.3). Pure conifer communities highest RIE (90.7 mm/yr), then pure deciduous (76.9). Mean tree height explained most variance (63.9% for ARI, then importance value; 44.4% for RIE, then crown width and planting density); diversity indices showed no correlation with RIE. Cites Xiao et al.: a maple intercepted 70.5% in the growing season vs 5.5% leafless
limits_noted: Authors: one survey month scaled to annual values; i-Tree species database North American; city-average weather; ground cover, grasses, shrubs and permeable paving ignored. Also: stemflow ignored; no field validation
relevance_to_topic: Modelled, not measured: tree size (height, crown width) dominates i-Tree interception, which is the allometric logic the tool would replace with LAI-based storage. Shows diversity does not drive interception, consistent with keeping diversity as a constraint only

citation: Techer & Berthier 2023 (Environ. Sci. Pollut. Res. 30:19705-19724)
file_in_papers: Techer 2023 - Vegetation-enhanced stormwater infiltration in bioretention systems.pdf
location: Review (16 documents, e.g. AU, US, FR; bioretention, rain gardens, biofilters)
method: Narrative review with a systematic Scopus search (1553 records, 835 articles, 11 retained, plus 5 grey documents); synthesis of plant type and root-trait effects on media hydraulic conductivity
traits_or_metrics: Saturated hydraulic conductivity, infiltration rate; root mass density, root diameter, root length density, specific root length, rooting depth; plant functional type
key_quantified_results: Infiltration gains rank turfgrass < prairie grass < shrubs < trees. Cited: tree seedlings kept infiltration 63% higher than bare compacted soil (up to 153%), red ash 27x (Bartens 2008); infiltration near plants about 50 mm/h higher, up to 170 mm/h (Virahsawmy 2014); prairie grass 37% vs turfgrass 10% runoff reduction in silty clay (model); Melaleuca ericifolia raised Ksat from 155 to 312 mm/h while Carex appressa did not (Le Coustumer 2012). Root mass density 0.1-2.2 kg/m3 linked to infiltration; macropores need roots of about 1-1.2 mm diameter; a 0.2 mm wider mean root diameter took infiltration from 2 to 10 cm/h for Juncus patens (Hart 2017). Biofilter media lose hydraulic conductivity early: mean -66% (521 to 176 mm/h) after 14 weeks in column tests, planted or not (Le Coustumer 2007; compaction, clogging); 30-40% of infiltration devices fail within a few years
limits_noted: Few studies, mostly columns and small rain gardens; no common metric; macropore bypass may reduce pollutant removal; tree evidence is mainly Bartens 2008 seedlings
relevance_to_topic: Root traits (thick, deep roots) raise infiltration, but evidence is from bioretention media, not street-tree pits; supports treating an infiltration bonus under trees as a cited ASSUMPTION rather than a species parameter. Complements Bartens (#16) and Zhang 2019 (#17)

citation: Zhao & Asawa 2026 (Urban For. Urban Green. 119:129366)
file_in_papers: Zhao 2026 - Urban isolated tree combined with ground covers for stormwater management.pdf
location: Aichi (lysimeter, 2010-2012) and Tokyo (annual scaling), JP; humid subtropical Cfa
method: Net rainfall under one Zelkova serrata (6.4 m, LAI 2.8-3.1, crown 5.5-9.2 m2) measured with a weighing lysimeter for 15 summer events (274.5 mm) and fed into SWMM as the rain-gauge input; tree pit as bio-retention LID calibrated on irrigation-drainage tests; roots modelled as 2.5x saturated conductivity (25 vs 10 mm/h); 8 cases: bare soil, impermeable, permeable and water-retaining pavements, each with and without the tree (pit about 10-18% of crown area)
traits_or_metrics: Interception loss, net rainfall, infiltration, storage, surface runoff, peak runoff, runoff delay; LAI, crown projection area; Ksat with and without roots
key_quantified_results: Tree vs bare soil: 4.6% less runoff in the three heavy events (crown interception 3.4%, roots 1.2%), 2.4% over all 15 events; interception about 45% of rain in two light events; peak cut at most 0.1 mm/min; runoff delayed 7 min. With surrounding pavement the tree cut runoff by 65.5% (impermeable), 12% (water-retaining), 0.4% (permeable). Annual Tokyo estimate: trees cut runoff about 2%, 70% and 8% vs soil, impermeable and water-retaining pavement alone; tree plus permeable pavement lowest runoff
limits_noted: Authors: one tree, measured net rainfall (not a crown storage model), 1-D SWMM without lateral flow or evaporation, runoff not validated against measured runoff, small planter limits roots, Tokyo only
relevance_to_topic: Shows how to bolt crown interception onto SWMM (net-rainfall input), the same gap the runoff module addresses; marginal tree benefit depends on the surface below (large over impervious, near zero over permeable paving), which supports placing trees over sealed ground in the layout optimiser

citation: Livesley, Baudinette & Glover 2014 (Urban For. Urban Green. 13:192-197)
file_in_papers: Livesley 2014 - Rainfall interception and stem flow by eucalypt street trees.pdf
location: Melbourne, AU (Burnley campus; May-Oct 2009, events 0.2-16 mm)
method: One mature Eucalyptus nicholii (dense canopy, rough bark) and one E. saligna (sparser, smooth bark): 0.72 m2 throughfall trough and stem helix to tipping buckets, rooftop gross-rain trough; PAI from cover photographs (k = 0.5); regressions of throughfall and stemflow on gross rain applied to hourly rain of 2008-2010
traits_or_metrics: Plant area index, crown porosity, bark type; canopy interception %, throughfall, stemflow, funnelling ratio
key_quantified_results: PAI 3.88 (E. nicholii) vs 3.03 (E. saligna). Interception for a 2 mm event >66% vs 36%; for 8 mm >46% vs 30%; little difference above 12 mm. Annual interception (2010, 680 mm) 44.4% vs 29.5%, i.e. about 100 mm less rain under the denser tree. Stemflow began at >1 mm (smooth) vs >=4 mm (rough); smooth-bark stemflow offsets only about 10 mm of the 200 mm intercepted; funnelling ratio 2.6 vs 0.2 (Results; the Discussion says 2.4). 31-37% of Melbourne's annual rain falls in events <=4 mm. Estimate: 30% canopy cover at PAI 4.0 cuts rain reaching a street by about 13%, approaching 20% with denser canopies; unpublished PAI of Platanus x acerifolia 5.5 (n = 7)
limits_noted: Two trees, one trough each, five winter-spring months, events only up to 16 mm; PAI from photographs with an assumed k; annual values extrapolated by regression
relevance_to_topic: Direct support for an LAI/PAI-scaled interception term and for saturation in large events; the 'canopy over impervious surfaces' framing matches the runoff module. Platanus PAI 5.5 is useful context for Barcelona's dominant street tree but is unpublished data

citation: Zabret, Rakovec & Sraj 2018 (J. Hydrol. 558:29-41)
file_in_papers: Zabret 2018 - Influence of meteorological variables on rainfall partitioning in urban area.pdf
method: Throughfall (roving funnels, troughs, tipping bucket) and stemflow under two Betula pendula and two Pinus nigra; 413 events (180 with disdrometer data); regression trees and boosted regression trees on 13 meteorological variables by phenoseason
traits_or_metrics: Interception loss, throughfall, stemflow by phenoseason; birch LAI 0.8 leafless / 2.6 leafed, pine LAI 3.9; bark storage 0.7 mm (birch) vs 3.5 mm (pine); branch angle; rainfall amount, intensity, duration, drop number and size, wind
key_quantified_results: Over 413 events (4110 mm) birch intercepted 888 mm and pine 1865 mm (about 22% and 45%). Mean event interception: pine 72% (leafed 72%, leafless 67%); birch 45% (leafed 51%, leafless 32%). Pine fully intercepted events below 1.1 mm and gave no throughfall below 1.3 mm; birch leafed interception fell from 50% to 31% for events longer than 6.7 h. Stemflow 1.2% of rain (birch) vs 0.02% (pine), starting above about 10.8 mm and 13.1 mm. Rainfall amount was the top variable, then intensity and drop number; smaller drops raised pine interception
limits_noted: Two trees per species at one site; wind from a station 3 km away; disdrometer data for 180 of 413 events; statistical (non-mechanistic) models
relevance_to_topic: Gives a measured leaf-on vs leaf-off interception contrast for a deciduous tree (about 51% vs 32% per event) and a deciduous-vs-evergreen conifer contrast, supporting the leaf-on calendar and evergreen weighting in season.py; temperate, not Mediterranean

citation: Alivio, Radinja, Sraj & Bezak 2025 (Urban For. Urban Green. 107:128792)
file_in_papers: Alivio 2025 - Stormwater runoff reduction of two distinct tree species.pdf
location: Ljubljana, SI (8.5 ha separate-sewer catchment, 76% impervious; plot data Aug 2021-Jun 2024)
method: SWMM with the Zi et al. 2021 tree-canopy LID module (Rutter/sparse-canopy interception, seasonal LAI), parameterised from a birch and a pine measured in a park (LAI-2200, throughfall troughs, stemflow, storage capacity by the Pereira method); catchment calibrated with NSGA-II on observed outlet flow (NSE 0.71); 240 trees at 15 m spacing as all-birch, all-pine or 50/50 mixed; 4 phenoseasons, 3 soils, events 15-291 mm
traits_or_metrics: LAI by phenoseason, canopy storage capacity Svmax, extinction coefficient (k = 0.7 assumed), crop coefficient, projected canopy area; runoff volume, peak flow, runoff coefficient, water balance
key_quantified_results: Measured: birch LAI 2.61 leafed / 0.95 leafless, Svmax 2.61 (text; 2.65 in Table 1) / 1.01 mm; pine LAI 3.72 / 2.25, Svmax 4.01 / 3.04 mm (about 1.00-1.08 mm per unit LAI when leafed, own calculation). Field interception 22.5% (birch) and 47.9% (pine) of gross rain. Model underestimated event interception by 3.1 points (birch) and 19.6 points (pine). Trees cut catchment runoff volume by 20-25% and peak flow by 16-25%; mixed planting best; extreme events less (90.3 mm: 14-16% volume, about 1.3% peak; 291 mm: 12-14%). Canopy interception up to 12.1% (birch), 21.1% (pine), 16.6% (mixed) of the water balance in small leafed-season events, under 5% above 60 mm; infiltration + storage under trees >20%. Trees over parking lots cut the runoff coefficient by 42.8% (leafed) and 50.0% (leafless) on average
limits_noted: Authors: k and crop coefficient generic, canopy parameters not calibrated, one size per species, pine interception underestimated, real events only (no design storms), temperate continental climate
relevance_to_topic: Closest runoff-module precedent: species LAI and canopy storage drive interception in SWMM, effect strongest over directly connected impervious areas and in small storms. Measured Svmax/LAI (about 1.0-1.1 mm) is a cross-check for the tool's s = 1.75 mm/LAI calibrated on Anys & Weiler 2024 (#1)

citation: Awad, Stanko, Barlokova, Ilavsky & Skultetyova 2026 (Water 18:2413)
file_in_papers: Awad 2026 - Machine learning surrogate modeling in R for green infrastructure screening.pdf
method: Proof-of-concept R workflow: 2000 synthetic catchment-storm-typology scenarios generated from prescribed closed-form equations (imperviousness 30-80%, return period 2/10/100 yr, coverage of bioretention, green roofs, permeable pavement, swales); linear regression, random forest and XGBoost trained to predict peak-flow attenuation and TSS reduction; 80/20 split, 5-fold CV
traits_or_metrics: Peak-flow attenuation, TSS reduction; R2, RMSE, MAE; feature importance; inference time
key_quantified_results: Held-out synthetic test set: XGBoost R2 0.96 and random forest 0.92 for peak attenuation (linear 0.90); 0.94 and 0.89 for TSS (linear 0.79). Inference about 2-4 ms per scenario vs a literature-typical 12-18 min per SWMM-LID run (not measured). Feature importance only reproduced the weights built into the generating equations. No SWMM runs or field data were used; the authors state it is not a validated hydrological surrogate
limits_noted: Authors: synthetic data only, illustrative typology weights, six features only, no same-hardware benchmark, retraining on SWMM-LID ensembles or monitored data required
relevance_to_topic: Low. Methodological reminder that a surrogate trained on synthetic equations only learns those equations; if the tool ever adds an ML surrogate it must be trained on its own runoff/heat model outputs. No trees, no heat

citation: Rezaei Aderyani, Jafarzadegan & Moradkhani 2025 (Sustain. Cities Soc. 123:106277)
file_in_papers: Rezaei Aderyani 2025 - Surrogate machine learning for urban flood modeling at metropolitan scales.pdf
location: Houston, Texas, US (city drainage network: 32,867 subcatchments, 66,482 manholes)
method: SWMM (dynamic wave) run on 2456 synthetic hyetographs built from 50 years of hourly NLDAS rain; network split into 363 clusters of connected manholes (threshold 20); per cluster, random forest surrogates predict manhole flood duration, peak and volume from 4 rainfall features (duration, depth, peak intensity, time to peak); tested on 6 real events incl. Hurricane Harvey
traits_or_metrics: Manhole surcharge duration, peak and volume; R2, RMSE; runtime
key_quantified_results: Single whole-city surrogate: R2 only 0.17-0.22. Clustered: validation R2 0.977 (duration), 0.846 (peak), 0.967 (volume); real-event test R2 0.844, 0.772, 0.729; Harvey R2 >0.8. Runtime for Harvey cut from 492.18 to 36.23 min (92.6%). Rainfall depth and duration were the most important features
limits_noted: Weaker on moderate events; synthetic hyetographs place rain randomly around the peak and may miss pre-peak loading; no land-cover or green-infrastructure inputs
relevance_to_topic: Low for the tree tool. Shows that surrogates of a drainage model need spatial partitioning and only learn rainfall-to-flood mapping, not the effect of surface interventions; no vegetation

citation: Willaredt, Velasquez-Camacho, Cinto Mejia, Singh & Ossola 2026 (Curr. Plant Biol. 47:100605)
file_in_papers: Willaredt 2026 - Effects of extreme climatic events on urban trees in Mediterranean regions.pdf
location: Review of Mediterranean-climate cities (Csa/Csb; 460 cities searched); included studies from Los Angeles, Santa Barbara, Santiago de Chile, Cuellar (ES), Cape Town, Lisbon, Naples, Florence
method: PRISMA systematic review (WoS, Scopus, Google Scholar; Jan 2025): over 3000 records, 127 assessed, 13 included; drought severity of each study compared with SPEI-6 from the Global SPEI Database
traits_or_metrics: Tree vigour (greenness, canopy cover), function (photosynthesis, stomatal closure, SLA), growth (tree rings), mortality; SPEI-6 drought severity
key_quantified_results: Only 13 studies, all since 2018; 43% from the US (Los Angeles, Santa Barbara). Remote sensing 53%, experiments 23%, field/dendrochronology 23%. Drought lowered NDVI (mean -0.023 in Los Angeles), canopy cover (-14% in one study, about -6% in another), photosynthesis (more in deciduous than evergreen trees) and SLA; drought-tolerant species grew and recovered better; irrigation raised growth but may reduce drought acclimation; no drought study reported mortality; one wind study (Lisbon) reported tree fall. No study considered soil properties; no Barcelona study
limits_noted: Few, heterogeneous studies (descriptive synthesis only); Koppen filter may miss near-Mediterranean cities; possible gaps in greenhouse work on Mediterranean species done elsewhere
relevance_to_topic: Supports drought and heat tolerance as hard constraints in the species palette for Barcelona and flags that leaf loss in drought cuts both shade and interception (season.py leaf-on calendar). Confirms there is no Barcelona-specific evidence on tree response to extremes

citation: Sciuto, Rizzo, Licciardello, Masi, Scavera, Barbagallo & Cirelli 2024 (16th International Conference on Urban Drainage, Delft, June 2024; poster and extended abstract)
file_in_papers: Sciuto 2024 - SuDS retrofitting for hydraulic risk mitigation in Catania (ICUD extended abstract).pdf; Sciuto 2024 - SuDS retrofitting for hydraulic risk mitigation in Catania (ICUD poster).pdf
read_level: full text (12 Oct; 4-page extended abstract and poster; DOI from the search record, not printed in the files)
location: Catania, Sicily, IT (Tondo Gioeni green areas, Andrea Doria Avenue)
method: Concept design (CARDIMED Horizon Europe demo): HEC-RAS hydraulic model on a 2 m DTM to map flood hazard (depth x (velocity + 0.5) + debris factor) and risk for 10/50/200-yr events; 4400 m2 retrofit with 4 lined bioretention cells, soakaways and infiltrating geo-cellular modules draining a 0.44 ha road
traits_or_metrics: Peak flow by return period, storage volume per impervious hectare, flood hazard and risk classes
key_quantified_results: Peak flow at the basin outlet 1.94, 7.24, 12.49, 25.69 and 38.13 m3/s for 2, 5, 10, 50 and 200-yr return periods (poster table). Bioretention area 960 m2 with 181 m3 storage, soakaways 7.5 m3, geo-cells 236 m3: about 426 m3 = 960 m3 per impervious ha, vs 300 (Catania 2014 rule) and 500 m3/ha (Sicily 2021 decree). Upstream catchment stated as about 30 ha in the extended abstract and about 110 ha on the poster. Construction by end 2025, monitoring 2025-2027
limits_noted: Concept design only; no performance results yet; vegetation and trees not modelled; inconsistent catchment area between the two documents
relevance_to_topic: Italian Mediterranean context for pluvial flooding and local hydraulic-invariance storage rules (m3 per impervious ha), a possible benchmark unit if the tool reports retained volume. No tree traits; low direct relevance

citation: Di Paola, Cimini, De Natale et al. 2026 (J. Hydrol. Reg. Stud. 63:103070; online Jan 2026)
file_in_papers: Di Paola 2026 - The May 2023 flood in Emilia-Romagna and 50-year trends in extreme precipitation.pdf
location: Emilia-Romagna, IT (284 rain gauges, 316 ERA5-Land grid points; 1974-2023)
method: Event analysis of May 2023 with rain gauges, ERA5 and ERA5-Land (soil moisture, storm surge at Porto Garibaldi); 50-year trend analysis of hourly ERA5-Land precipitation (99th-percentile extremes, persistence, wet area, space-time events, ETCCDI indices) with Theil-Sen and Mann-Kendall
traits_or_metrics: Event accumulations, hourly intensities, soil water content, flooded area; trends in intensity, frequency, wet hours, persistence, fragmentation of extremes
key_quantified_results: Two persistent, mostly stratiform events: 1-3 May (gauge peaks 273, 259, 231 mm in 42 h) and 16-17 May (260, 255, 254 mm in 36 h), with hourly accumulations generally below 5-7 mm. Soils near saturation (above the 99th percentile) at the start of the 16-17 May event; storm surge above 0.8 m hindered drainage; flooded area up to 125,174 ha (about 5.6% of the region; Cremonini #61 gives about 58 km2, so the sources disagree), depths up to 5.5 m; losses about EUR 8.8 billion (text; abstract 'exceeding EUR 8 billion'). Trends 1974-2023: 1-h extreme accumulations +10% (consistent with Clausius-Clapeyron for +1.3 C), up to 2-h +5%; frequency of extremes up to 3 h +26%; fewer wet hours, more fragmented rain; intensity-defined extreme events +9% in magnitude and +61% in frequency
limits_noted: Authors: ERA5-Land biases (underestimates gauge peaks, about 360 vs 600 mm), possible non-stationarities; 99th-percentile approach not suited to rarer events like May 2023
relevance_to_topic: Confirms May 2023 in Emilia-Romagna was a saturated-soil, river-overflow (fluvial/mixed) disaster driven by long low-intensity rain, not urban pluvial runoff where street trees matter; but short-duration extremes are rising. Supports framing the tool around frequent short pluvial storms and keeping Bologna as context only (see Cremonini #61)

citation: Zhu, Xu, Liu, Yin, Jia & Guan 2023 (Resour. Conserv. Recycl. 191:106906)
file_in_papers: Zhu 2023 - Spatial layout optimization of green infrastructure with life-cycle MOO and SWMM.pdf
location: Tongzhou, Beijing sub-centre, CN (Sponge City pilot, 19.36 km2; temperate monsoon, 536 mm/yr)
method: SWMM (calibrated NSE 0.66/0.92, validated 0.62/0.71) coupled with NSGA-II (population 100, 100 generations) choosing GI type and area per subcatchment (permeable pavement, sunken green space, bioretention, vegetated swale) under area caps; objectives: max runoff control capacity (volume + peak + flooded-node reduction), min life-cycle investment cost (15 yr), max monetised economic-environmental-social benefit; 2-h Chicago design storms of 3, 5 and 10 yr; Pareto set screened by three decision-maker preferences
traits_or_metrics: Runoff volume, peak and flooded-node reduction; life-cycle cost (RMB/m2); monetised benefits (pollutant removal, groundwater recharge, land value)
key_quantified_results: Life-cycle cost per m2: permeable pavement 832, vegetated swale 581, sunken green space 1270, bioretention 1580 RMB. Total runoff control rate about 89% on average (target 84%). Recommended 10-yr layout: cost 5.7-7.6 billion RMB, benefit 8.1-9.0 million RMB per design storm; permeable pavement 26-38% of GI area across preferences. Ecological-restoration benefit was over 60% of monetised benefit, economic benefits under 1%. GI placed first in high-imperviousness zones when cost is constrained. The paper reports GI area both as about 610-625 ha (30% of the area) and as 55-70 ha, which is inconsistent
limits_noted: Authors: cost data uncertain, short design storms only, no full sensitivity analysis; no trees; equal weights in the runoff index
relevance_to_topic: Method precedent for coupling a runoff model with NSGA-II and screening the Pareto front by stakeholder preference, as planned for the layout optimiser (weighted sum first, NSGA-II later). No vegetation traits or heat; GI types, not trees

citation: Stovin, Jorgensen & Clayden 2008 (Arboric. J. 30:297-310)
file_in_papers: Stovin 2008 - Street trees and stormwater management.pdf
location: Sheffield, UK (Heeley, 39 ha; two residential morphology units)
method: Narrative review of street-tree hydrology and North American canopy-stormwater valuation (American Forests CITYgreen), plus a GIS case study: tree canopy (>3 m) traced on aerial photos for Victorian terraces and 1930s semi-detached housing; qualitative options for new planting
traits_or_metrics: Tree canopy cover, impermeable cover, housing density; cited interception losses
key_quantified_results: Tree cover 6% (Victorian terraces, 56% impermeable) and 13% (1930s semi-detached, 31% impermeable). Cited: interception 10-40% of annual rain (Xiao et al. 2000 review), pear 15% vs cork oak 27%; a Toronto study assuming 2 mm (about 40%) interception per event estimated 10-20% less annual runoff when cover rises from about 25% to 50%; trees intercept best in small storms, so their role may be larger for water quality than for flooding. No hydraulic modelling yet
limits_noted: Preliminary; no runoff modelling; cited figures largely from grey literature (CUFR, American Forests); case-study table units unclear in the extracted text
relevance_to_topic: Early framing of street trees as retrofit SuDS over impervious surfaces and of the small-storm limitation; secondary, mostly cited numbers

citation: Schooling & Carlyle-Moses 2015 (Urban Ecosyst. 18:1261-1284)
file_in_papers: Schooling 2015 - Rainfall depth class and deciduous tree traits on stemflow production.pdf
location: Kamloops, British Columbia, CA (irrigated urban park; semi-arid, 278 mm/yr; Jun 2012-Nov 2013, leaf-on)
method: Stemflow collars on 37 isolated deciduous trees of 21 species (20 single-leader, 17 multi-leader; DBH 10-69 cm); 86 events (327.9 mm, over 80% <5 mm) in 4 depth classes; 34 traits (branch angles, leader count, bark relief index, canopy and wood cover, size); stepwise multiple regression per class
traits_or_metrics: Stemflow % of rain on the projected canopy, funnelling ratio; branch angle, leader number, bark relief, DBH, canopy height-to-width ratio, canopy and wood cover
key_quantified_results: Stemflow negligible below 2 mm; group means 0.8-0.9% (2-5 mm), 2.0-2.8% (5-10 mm), 2.7-3.1% (>=10 mm). Event maxima 22.8% (columnar English oak, 25.6 mm) and funnelling ratio 196.9 (Riversii European beech). Regression r2 0.44-0.92 per class; steep branch angles, multiple leaders and smooth bark (deeply furrowed bark for single-leader trees above 10 mm) raised stemflow; large trees (DBH >30 cm) produced little because small storms do not exceed their storage threshold
limits_noted: One park, leaf-on season only, irrigated semi-arid site; high event-to-event variability; interception and throughfall not measured
relevance_to_topic: Stemflow is a small share of rain on average (a few %) but concentrates water at the tree base; supports ignoring stemflow in a v1 interception term while noting pit infiltration capacity. Branch angle and bark are secondary traits, not core palette parameters

citation: Nooraei Beidokhti & Moore 2021 (Urban For. Urban Green. 60:127052)
file_in_papers: Nooraei Beidokhti 2021 - Precipitation, phenology, LAI and bark effects on throughfall by urban trees.pdf
location: Meta-analysis: 8 urban studies (US, Mexico, Canada, Australia, Slovenia, Puerto Rico)
method: Meta-regression of 396 event-scale throughfall observations from open-grown urban trees (data digitised); linear throughfall-vs-rain models by leaf type and phenology (evergreen broadleaf, evergreen needleleaf, deciduous leafed, deciduous leafless), ANCOVA by bark texture; LAI effect on study-level throughfall ratio (n = 10 trees) and a multiple regression with rain depth
traits_or_metrics: Throughfall vs event rain depth; leaf type, phenology, bark roughness, LAI; interception and stemflow % per study
key_quantified_results: Throughfall slopes: needleleaf evergreen 0.53 (Table 3; abstract and conclusion say 0.56), deciduous leafless 0.81, deciduous leafed 0.86, evergreen broadleaf 0.80; leafless trees start throughfall at lower rain depth (intercept), implying leaf storage of about 1.5-4 mm; leafless deciduous trees still capture nearly 20% of rain. Smooth-barked leafless trees give more throughfall than rough-barked ones. Throughfall ratio falls non-linearly with LAI, mostly above LAI 2.5; rain depth dominates (standardised coefficient 0.94 vs -0.08 for LAI; R2 0.93). Study means of interception range from 14.3% to 72%
limits_noted: Only 8 studies, rain depth as the sole storm variable, LAI as one leaf-on value, bark classes coarse, uneven data by tree type
relevance_to_topic: Gives first-order throughfall equations by leaf type and confirms LAI matters but saturates; supports a leaf-type split (needleleaf evergreen vs broadleaf) in the palette and a non-zero leaf-off interception for deciduous trees in season.py

citation: Asadian & Weiler 2009 (Water Qual. Res. J. Can. 44:16-25)
file_in_papers: Asadian 2009 - A new approach in measuring rainfall interception by urban trees in coastal British Columbia.pdf
location: North Vancouver, British Columbia, CA (streets, parks, forest control; Oct 2007-Jun 2008)
method: Throughfall under 6 urban conifers (Douglas-fir, western red cedar; dominant, codominant, single, forest control) with two slotted 3 m PVC pipes per tree draining to a tipping bucket; rooftop gross-rain units of the same design; stemflow assumed negligible; 7 events (377 mm; max 13.3 mm/h, about a 2-yr intensity)
traits_or_metrics: Event interception loss %, throughfall, throughfall delay and intensity; tree type and health
key_quantified_results: Mean interception 49.1% (Douglas-fir) and 60.9% (western red cedar) over 7 events; per tree and event 5-98% (1.5-24.3 mm). Throughfall delayed by up to 6-7.5 h in a 39.7 mm, 39-h event and up to 8.5-45.5 h in event 1; throughfall intensity occasionally exceeded rainfall intensity (drip). Authors conclude urban conifer interception is about twice that of forest conifers (9-48% in temperate forests)
limits_noted: Six trees, seven events, stemflow ignored, many events lost to clogging and frost; 'twice forest values' comparison is across studies, not paired
relevance_to_topic: Upper bound for evergreen conifer interception in long, low-intensity frontal rain; not representative of Barcelona's short convective storms. Supports separating conifers in the palette; frequently cited by later urban interception studies

citation: Kermavnar & Vilhar 2017 (Urban Ecosyst. 20:1373-1387)
file_in_papers: Kermavnar 2017 - Canopy precipitation interception in urban forests in relation to stand structure.pdf
location: Ljubljana, SI (three 0.25 ha urban forest plots; 2008-2013)
method: Bulk precipitation in adjacent open areas and throughfall under the canopy (fixed funnels and gutters, fortnightly or monthly) in a mixed upland forest (oak, chestnut, Norway spruce), a riparian Scots pine forest and a floodplain hardwood forest; stemflow estimated from literature weighted by species basal area; leafed vs leafless seasons
traits_or_metrics: Stand-level canopy interception, throughfall, estimated stemflow (% of bulk precipitation); canopy cover, conifer share, basal area, growing stock; hourly rain intensity
key_quantified_results: Annual interception 18.0% (mixed forest: 90-100% canopy cover, 46% evergreen conifers, 589 m3/ha), 7.1% (floodplain hardwood) and 3.9% (riparian pine, about 50% cover). limits_noted: Stemflow not measured; monthly or fortnightly sampling; few collectors in two plots; bulk rain 100 m outside each stand
relevance_to_topic: Stand-scale (urban forest) values, much lower than isolated-tree studies; canopy cover and conifer share drive interception. Context only for street trees; shows interception drops when summer storms are intense

citation: Colaninno, Salvati, Lopez-Besora & Morganti 2025 (Sustain. Cities Soc. 130:106498)
file_in_papers: Colaninno 2025 - District-scale cumulative heat stress mapping using very-high-resolution spatiotemporal simulation.pdf (OA copy, polimi repository; not in papers/)
location: Barcelona (Gracia district; plazas Joanic, Revolucio, Rovira), ES
method: SOLWEIG (UMEP) at 1 m from LiDAR DSM; tree canopy transmissivity tau_I tested at 3%, 10%, 20% x isotropic/anisotropic sky (6 runs); black-globe (PCE-WB 20SD, +-0.6 C), air T, wind at 1.5 m, 26 Jul 2022 11-13 h and 28 Aug 2022 6-7:30 h; Tmrt from globe by the ASHRAE equation
traits_or_metrics: Tmrt, tau_I

limits_noted: 3 plazas, 2 short campaigns, 30 and 20 min each; one shaded point; calibration on the same points it is judged on; data only on request; no species LAI
relevance_to_topic: Only Barcelona sun/shade Tmrt measurement with tau sensitivity found; 10% tau for Platanus rows is the closest local value; direct ancestor of our tau calibration check

citation: Ibrahim, Kershaw & Shepherd 2020 (BSO-V 2020, IBPSA-England; Loughborough)
file_in_papers: Ibrahim 2020 - Improvement of the Ladybug-tools microclimate workflow a verification study.pdf (OA, publications.ibpsa.org; not in papers/)
location: Cairo (hot arid) and London; hypothetical canyons
method: Modified Ladybug-tools Python source (ground reflectivity, radiative heat transfer coefficient, projected area factor, reflected radiation; view-factor-weighted longwave) verified against ENVI-met 4.4.4; no trees, no field data

citation: Santamour 1990 (METRIA 7 Proceedings, pp. 57-65)
file_in_papers: Santamour 1990 - Trees for urban planting diversity, uniformity, and common sense.pdf
method: Position paper (expert guidance, no data)
traits_or_metrics: Relative abundance of the most common species / genus / family
key_quantified_results: Proposes the 10-20-30 rule: no more than 10% of any species, 20% of any genus, 30% of any family (p. 64). Says he does not know who first proposed the 10% rule (p. 58) and that the species rule 'offers little protection' because pests follow genera and families; generic diversity is most important (pp. 62-63). Names sycamore anthracnose on Platanus (p. 58), fire blight, to which Rosaceae genera incl. Pyrus (mostly P. calleryana) are 'potentially susceptible' (p. 63), and Sophora among the legume genera (p. 63). Recommends scattered 'blocks of uniformity' of proven species (pp. 57, 64)
limits_noted: No empirical basis given for the thresholds; North American pest examples
relevance_to_topic: Origin of the cap family Barcelona's 15% belongs to. Barcelona caps species only, while Santamour argues genus and family matter more: Tipuana and Styphnolobium are both legumes (Fabaceae), Pyrus is Rosaceae (fire blight). Cite for the rationale of the cap and for a family-level check of the palette

citation: Kendal, Dobbs & Lohr 2014 (Urban For. Urban Green. 13:411-417)
file_in_papers: Kendal 2014 - Global patterns of diversity in the urban forest Is there evid.pdf
method: Comparison of urban forest inventories by Koppen climate group and land use; relative abundance of the most common taxon vs Shannon index
traits_or_metrics: Relative abundance of the most common species, genus and family; Shannon index
key_quantified_results: Most-common-species share is far above Santamour's 10% in every climate group; the 10% benchmark is near the global 10th percentile, genus median 22% overall (21% outside Continental/Arid climates, 29% Continental, 25% Arid) and family 27-32%, closer to 20/30. Streetscapes are less diverse than parks (genus median 24% vs 15%). Earlier benchmarks were 5% (Barker 1975), then 'mostly 10-15%' (Grey & Deneke 1986; Santamour 1990; Miller & Miller 1991; Raupp et al. 2006). Warns that targets substantially below existing abundance risk abandoning well-adapted species for underperforming ones and changing ecosystem services (p. 415, citing Richards 1993); the stronger 'reduction in ecosystem service benefits' wording (p. 415) is about Continental streetscapes, and for Temperate climates benchmarks may need lowering
limits_noted: Inventories of different extent and date; the authors say the risk-diversity relationship itself is not established
relevance_to_topic: Gives the 15% its lineage (10-15% range in the literature) and directly supports the v6 problem: a diversity cap applied without performance data can trade away ecosystem services. Also says benchmarks should differ by land use (higher for streetscapes)
